# Conclusion and Future Work

This study found only modest evidence of clustering structure in the learned MovieLens user embeddings. None of the methods produced uniformly strong results across embedding dimensions and evaluation criteria, and several of the selected solutions showed weak separation or poor reproducibility. The strongest evidence came from K-means and Reduced K-means, which at least showed a consistent tendency toward nontrivial partition structure, especially in the 128-dimensional embeddings. Even there, however, the silhouette values remained moderate rather than strong, so the results support only a cautious claim that the embeddings contain some cluster tendency rather than clear, well-separated latent groups.

Under the method-specific selection criteria, Reduced K-means produced the strongest overall hard-clustering results. Its best model used the 128-dimensional embeddings, 2 clusters, and 4 retained factors, and it achieved the highest ordinary silhouette among the selected models. K-means remained competitive and agreed strongly with Reduced K-means in the partition-comparison analysis, which suggests that both methods recovered roughly the same low-dimensional structure. At the same time, the revised K-means rule based on the within-cluster sum of squares elbow selected 4-cluster solutions whose silhouette values were clearly weaker than the corresponding 2-cluster solutions. That disagreement shows that the K-means conclusion depends materially on the tuning rule and weakens any strong substantive interpretation of the selected K-means models.

The probabilistic methods provided even less convincing evidence. PD clustering remained fast but produced ordinary silhouette values near zero and showed little bootstrap reproducibility. FPDC improved the probability-silhouette criterion relative to PD, but it still produced weak or negative ordinary silhouette values, low agreement with K-means and Reduced K-means, and substantially higher computational cost. The FPDC sensitivity analysis also showed that changing the tuning parameter $\nu$ could alter the selected model without producing a clearly better hard partition. Taken together, these results do not support FPDC or PD clustering as strong practical choices for these embeddings.


The main positive conclusion is therefore narrow. The learned MovieLens user embeddings appear to contain some clustering tendency, and K-means and Reduced K-means both detect it most clearly in the 128-dimensional representation. The broader conclusion is more cautious: the evidence does not support a claim of strong, sharply separated user clusters, and the final interpretation depends nontrivially on how model selection prioritizes elbow diagnostics, silhouette width, probability silhouette, and stability.


The results also showed that embedding dimension mattered. The 128-dimensional embeddings produced the clearest and most separable structure, followed by the 256-dimensional embeddings and then the 64-dimensional embeddings. This pattern suggests that 64 dimensions compressed the latent user-preference structure too aggressively, while 256 dimensions retained useful structure but did not improve separation beyond the 128-dimensional representation. 

The study brings together partition-based clustering, dimension reduction, latent-factor methods, and cluster validation within a representation-learning framework. Although recommendation performance is not evaluated, the resulting cluster structure may still be relevant to downstream tasks such as personalization, interpretation, and content organization.

Future work should test whether other clustering methods are better suited to this kind of recommendation-data embedding. In particular, spectral clustering could capture non-spherical structure that K-means may miss; Gaussian mixture models could assess whether overlapping elliptical groups provide a better description than centroid-based partitions; hierarchical clustering could reveal nested structure rather than forcing a single flat partition; and density-based methods such as DBSCAN or HDBSCAN could test whether the embeddings contain small dense groups embedded in a large diffuse background rather than a few global clusters. For recommender-system embeddings specifically, future work could also examine community-detection methods on user similarity graphs, mixture models designed for latent-factor spaces, and clustering methods that explicitly account for sparsity, uncertainty, or soft membership. A stronger next step would combine these alternative clustering approaches with richer representation learning, such as autoencoders, matrix-factorization embeddings, or graph neural recommender embeddings, and then evaluate whether any method yields more stable, better-separated, and more interpretable user segments.
